paper_title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference Mobina Kashaniyan and Ali Jannesari Department of Computer Science Iowa State University, USA {mobina, jannesar}@iastate.edu AbstractTest-time scaling (TTS) improves the reasoning of large language models (LLMs) by generating several samples for query and voting on the answer. However, fixed sampling budget ignores two facts: different queries need different amounts of reasoning, and the cost of one more sample changes with GPU load. In our measurements, the same four-sample query uses up to 4.1 more energy when other jobs load the GPU. Existing adaptive methods mainly set the budget from answer agreement, question structure, or question difficulty. They decide how much reasoning query needs, but not what that reasoning costs on the GPU right now. We present ATEST, runtime framework for resource-aware TTS with two modes. Its default mode, ATEST-Online, needs no offline calibration: it starts with one sample, checks whether the plurality answer is stable, reads the live GPU state, predicts the cost of the next step with an online cost model, and decides whether to stop or continue. For stable deployments that can reuse one-time profile, ATEST also offers an offline mode, ATEST-Calibrated, which picks the budget from accuracy and cost models built offline. We evaluate ATEST with Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 across four reasoning and question-answering datasets under controlled idle-to-high GPU load schedule, and repeat the study on an NVIDIA L40S and with second model, Qwen2.5-3B. On the A100, ATEST-Online answers every query, never exceeds the energy budget, gives the highest or statistically tied accuracy on all four datasets, and uses fewer samples as load rises. The same pattern holds on the L40S and with Qwen2.5-3B, where ATEST-Online again answers every query within the budget. On GSM8K at high load, it keeps 60.0% accuracy, while ATEST-Calibrated drops to 44.0% because it defers 42.4% of the queries. controlled ablation shows that online cost learning is what makes the budget follow the load. Including offline calibration, ATEST-Online uses 42 less GPU time and 48 less energy than ATEST-Calibrated. Its main costs are higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks, and offline calibration remains strong only when the load is stable. These results show that TTS on shared GPUs is runtime resource-management problem, not only an accuracy problem. Index Termslarge language models, test-time scaling, GPU load, resource-aware inference, adaptive sampling, energy-aware systems I. INTRODUCTION Large language models (LLMs) give better answers when they use more computation at inference time. simple and popular way to do this is test-time scaling (TTS) with voting: the model generates several answers (samples) for the same question, and the system returns the most common one [1], [2]. More samples usually mean better answers, but they also mean more GPU work, more energy, and longer waiting time. Fig. 1. The idea of ATEST. Standard test-time scaling (TTS) generates the same number of samples for query whether the GPU is idle or busy. ATEST looks at the live GPU load. When the GPU is busy and each sample costs more energy, it skips samples that are not worth their cost. Because of this cost, recent work makes TTS adaptive. These methods give more samples to hard queries and fewer to easy ones, using signals such as answer agreement, query difficulty, or reasoning progress [3][8]. They answer one question well: how many samples does this query need? However, they treat the cost of one sample as fixed number. On real system, this cost is not fixed. LLM performance depends on batching, scheduling, and memory management [9], [10], and the same number of samples can have very different energy, latency, and throughput costs [11]. Many GPUs in clusters and HPC centers are shared: other jobs run on the same GPU at the same time and compete with the LLM for compute, memory bandwidth, and power, and this competition changes over time. In our measurements on an A100, the same four-sample query uses up to 4.1 more energy when the GPU is heavily loaded  (Fig. 3)  . For example, GSM8K query costs 121.7 on an idle GPU and 455.6 on busy one. controller that ignores this change either wastes energy when the GPU is busy, or uses up its energy budget too early and must defer later queries, which means refusing to answer them.

sections.title: So a TTS controller on a shared GPU must answer two
sections.content: questions at the same time: 1) Is one more sample useful for this query? Fig. 2. Overview of ATEST. (a) Standard TTS generates fixed number of samples and does not use the live GPU state. (b) ATEST-Calibrated, the offline mode of ATEST, builds accuracy and cost models offline for each dataset and picks once per query. (c) ATEST-Online starts with one sample and adds samples step by step (1 3 4 6 8). (d) An illustration of one decision: 1 Monte Carlo look-ahead to Bmax = 8 estimates how likely the current winner is to stay the winner, and is how much the next step raises this; 2 the online cost model learns from the measured energy of every step, follows the load, and predicts the next steps energy with safety margin; 3 with the same votes, ATEST-Online continues on an idle GPU but stops on busy one. 2) What does that sample cost on the GPU right now? We present ATEST, resource-aware TTS framework that answers both questions. Fig. 1 shows the idea: when the GPU is busy, ATEST skips samples that are not worth their higher cost. ATEST has two modes that share the same budget ladder, GPU monitor, and energy accounting  (Fig. 2)  . Its default mode, ATEST-Online, needs no offline profiling. It works as closed control loop: it generates samples in small steps, checks whether the vote is becoming stable, reads the live GPU state, measures what each step really cost, updates an online cost model, and stops as soon as another step is not worth its cost. Some deployments, however, run the same model and workload on GPU whose load rarely changes, or need low tail latency. For these cases ATEST also offers an offline mode, ATEST-Calibrated, which profiles each dataset once and picks the whole budget per query from accuracy and cost models, together with the live GPU state. Choosing once lets it generate all samples in one batch, which gives lower tail latency and higher throughput on short tasks. The price is the profile itself, which took 5.73 GPU-hours and 7.16 MJ for our four datasets, and cost model that does not follow the GPU when the load changes. Including profiling, ATESTOnline uses 42 less GPU time and 48 less energy than ATEST-Calibrated on the same 2,000 queries. This difference matters most when the GPU becomes busy. On GSM8K under high load, ATEST-Calibrated must defer 42.4% of the queries, so it answers only 44.0% of them correctly. Under the same load, ATEST-Online answers every query, keeps 60.0% accuracy, and uses less energy per query (175.8 vs. 206.4 J). Across all four datasets, ATEST-Online never defers query, never exceeds the energy budget, and gives the highest or tied-best accuracy. We also test why ATESTOnline changes its budget. In controlled ablation, we keep the remaining-energy signal fixed, so that budget depletion cannot drive the decision. Without online cost learning, the controller uses the same mean budget (B = 3.12) at every load level on all four datasets. With online cost learning, the budget follows the load. So the adaptation comes from the runtime resource signals, not from the budget running out. Contributions. This paper makes three contributions: 1) We show with measurements that the cost of TTS sample is not fixed: on GPU shared with other jobs, the same four-sample query uses up to 4.1 more energy under high load. Based on this, we treat adaptive TTS as runtime resource-management problem, where each decision weighs the value of more reasoning against its current cost. 2) We introduce ATEST with two modes. Its default mode, ATEST-Online, learns the cost of sampling online and decides step by step, with no dataset-specific profiling. Its offline mode, ATEST-Calibrated, picks the budget once from offline accuracy and cost models together with the live GPU state, for deployments that can reuse one-time profile. 3) We show when each mode should be used. Under changing load, ATEST-Online answers every query and stays within the energy budget, while ATEST-Calibrated defers up to 42.4% of the queries. Under stable load, offline calibration remains strong choice. controlled ablation shows that online cost learning is what makes the budget follow the load. II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK A. Test-Time Scaling and Adaptive Sampling Test-time scaling (TTS) uses more computation at inference time to get better answers [12]. common form is to generate several answers for the same query and combine them. Chainof-thought prompting [1], [13], [14] lets the model write out its reasoning, and self-consistency [2], [15] samples several reasoning paths and returns the answer that appears most often. We call the number of samples the sampling budget B. The same budget is not useful for every query. Easy questions are often answered correctly after one or two samples, while hard questions may need more. Adaptive methods therefore change per query. Adaptive-Consistency [3], [16] and EarlyStopping Self-Consistency [4], [17], [18][20] stop sampling once the answers agree. Other methods use question difficulty, answer confidence, or reasoning progress [5][8]. These methods remove many unnecessary samples. However, they decide only from the reasoning side: they ask whether more samples would change the answer, but not what those samples cost on the GPU right now. Recent work shows that the number of samples alone does not describe the systems cost of TTS, because the same samples can have very different energy, latency, and throughput costs depending on how they run [11]. ATEST adds this missing systems side to adaptive TTS. B. GPU-Aware and Energy-Efficient LLM Serving LLM serving systems [21], [22] show that runtime conditions strongly affect inference performance. Orca [9] and vLLM [10] improve batching and GPU memory management. Llumnix [23] moves requests between model instances at runtime to balance load and reduce latency, and Bullet [24] changes GPU resource allocation during execution based on current performance conditions. Energy is also main goal in LLM serving. Samsi et al. [25] measured the energy cost of LLM inference on V100 and A100 GPUs. POLCA [26] studies power management and power oversubscription in LLM clusters, and DynamoLLM [27] reconfigures inference clusters to save energy while meeting latency targets. throttLLeM [28] adjusts GPU frequency and resource configuration to reduce inference energy while meeting latency targets. EnerTune [29] studies energy-aware GPU sharing, models how GPU allocation, frequency, and batch size affect power and performance, and shows that large profiling spaces can make offline profiling expensive. These systems decide how to run given amount of work: where to place requests, how to batch them, and how to set the hardware. They do not decide how much reasoning work each query should get. ATEST makes this second decision, so it complements these systems and can run on top of them. C. Research Gap Adaptive TTS decides how much reasoning query needs but treats the cost of sample as fixed, while inference and energy systems manage the GPU but do not change how much reasoning each query gets. On shared GPU, these decisions depend on each other: one more sample is worth it only if the answers so far and the current GPU cost justify it. No prior method in Table reads the live GPU state; the closest, Adaptive-Cal [8], uses offline-calibrated models. ATEST makes TABLE FAMILIES OF TTS METHODS. INDENTED ROWS ARE THE METHODS WE RUN. Motivation. (a) Energy per answered query for fixed budget of = 4 at four GPU load levels, relative to idle. The value under each level is the measured GPU utilization. (b) Error of the offline cost model, averaged over four datasets. Without live GPU state (Adaptive-Cal), the error grows from 26% at idle to 283% at high load. Adding live GPU state (ATEST-Calibrated) lowers the high-load error to 55%, but the error is still large at medium load (130%). this decision at runtime using both signals, and ATEST-Online learns the cost online without per-dataset profiling. III. MOTIVATION When several jobs share one GPU, they compete for the same compute units, memory bandwidth, and power limit. As result, the same microbatch runs longer, and the GPU draws more power while it runs. In our setup, each microbatch is charged for the GPU energy used while it occupies the GPU (VI), so the same number of samples costs more joules when the GPU is busy. This cost depends on the current load, which changes over time and is not known in advance. Fig. 3 shows two observations from our experiments. Observation 1: the same budget can cost several times more. With fixed budget of = 4, the energy per answered query rises with load on all four datasets. At high load it is 3.7 the idle value on GSM8K and MATH, and 4.1 on ARC-Challenge. Observation 2: an offline cost model does not follow the load. cost model fitted offline predicts the cost of budget before it runs. Fig. 3(b) shows that its prediction error grows quickly as the GPU becomes busy. Adding the live GPU state as an input helps, but it does not remove the problem.

sections.title: These observations lead to four design goals for a TTS
sections.content: controller on shared GPU: G1 Spend samples where they help. Give more samples only to queries whose answer is still uncertain. G2 Follow the live cost. Use the cost of sample now, not the cost measured during profiling. G3 Avoid expensive profiling. Do not require new offline calibration for every dataset. G4 Stay safe and serve everyone. Never exceed the energy budget, and avoid deferring queries. ATEST-Calibrated meets G1, partly meets G2, and does not meet G3. ATEST-Online is designed to meet all four. IV. PROBLEM FORMULATION We serve stream of queries q1, . . . , qN on one GPU that is shared with other jobs. For each query qi, the controller chooses budget Bi = {1, 3, 4, 6, 8}. The GPU condition at time is Ht. Because Ht changes, the same budget can have different energy cost at different times. All queries share one energy budget Emax. So deferring is never free: it protects the budget, but it lowers accuracy and coverage. V. ATESTDESIGN A. Overview ATEST has two modes that share the same budget ladder, GPU monitor (NVML [30]), and energy accounting. They differ in when they decide and what they learn. The default mode, ATEST-Online, decides step by step, using the samples it has already generated and cost model that it learns while it runs. The offline mode, ATEST-Calibrated, decides the whole budget once, before generating any sample, using models built offline. Table II summarizes the differences. When to use the offline mode. ATEST-Online is the right choice when the load changes or new models and datasets arrive often. ATEST-Calibrated is useful in three cases: (1) the model, GPU, and workload stay the same long enough to reuse one profile, where it reaches higher accuracy under stable load (VII-F); (2) the service needs low tail latency or high throughput on short tasks, since it generates all samples in one batch (VII-E); and (3) the cost of each query must be known before it runs. ATEST-Online continues only if the next step is worth its cost and fits in the budget: Einc γ and Einc Erem, (9) where γ is minimum gain per joule and Erem is the remaining energy budget. It also stops when the answer is already stable, when more samples are unlikely to resolve disagreement, or when it reaches Bmax. simple example. The following case is only an illustration of the rule. Suppose math question has three samples, and all three give the answer 42. The vote is already stable, so is close to zero and ATEST-Online stops at = 3, whether the GPU is idle or busy. Now suppose the three samples give 42, 42, and 40. More samples could still change the winner, so is large. If the GPU is idle, the next step is cheap, U/Einc passes the threshold, and ATEST-Online goes to = 4. If the GPU is busy, the same step costs several times more joules (Fig. 3(a)), the ratio can drop below γ, and ATESTOnline returns 42. In both cases the decision uses the same two questions: is the next sample useful, and what does it cost now? Two feedback loops. Each executed step feeds back twice. The new answers update the reasoning signal , and the measured energy updates the cost model. So the next decision depends on both how the reasoning is going and how the GPU is behaving now. Overhead. The controller runs on the host CPU. Per step, it reads NVML, runs small Monte Carlo estimate, and does one RLS update. The main runtime cost is not this computation, but the fact that samples are generated in several smaller steps instead of one batch (VII-E). C. ATEST-Calibrated ATEST-Calibrated is the offline mode of ATEST. We call it Calibrated because its accuracy and cost models come from an offline calibration (profiling) phase; it still serves queries at runtime and reads the live GPU state, but its models stay fixed. For each dataset, we run 500 calibration prompts at each of the five budgets and four load levels (20 settings). Since the five budgets together use 1 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 22 samples per prompt, this generates 500 22 4 = 44,000 samples per dataset. The calibration prompts come from separate split and do not overlap with the evaluation queries. From these runs we fit two models. The accuracy model ˆP (q, B) estimates the chance that budget gives correct answer for query q, using query features such as estimated difficulty. The cost model ˆE(B, H) predicts the energy of budget under GPU condition by predicting its power and run time and multiplying them, since energy is power times time (watts seconds = joules). Both models stay fixed after this phase. Online phase. For each query, ATEST-Calibrated reads the current GPU state Ht. For an upgrade from budget to the next budget B, it computes the expected accuracy gain and the extra energy: ˆP = ˆP (q, B) ˆP (q, B), ˆE = ˆE(B, Ht) ˆE(B, Ht). (10) (11) The score ˆP / ˆE is the expected gain per extra joule. The allocator first gives the query the smallest budget. Then, among the upgrades on the ladder 1 3 4 6 8 that still fit in the remaining energy, it takes the one with the best score. It stops when no useful upgrade fits. If even = 1 does not fit according to the cost model, the query is deferred. After this, all samples are generated and the plurality answer is returned. The generated samples do not change the chosen budget. Weakness. ATEST-Calibrated uses the live GPU state, but its cost model was learned from the profiling runs and is never updated. When the real cost moves away from the model, the allocator either overspends early or rejects queries that it could have served. VI. EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY We evaluate ATEST under controlled GPU load. Our goal is to measure both answer quality and system behavior as the GPU condition changes. A. Model, Hardware, and Settings We use Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct [32] in bfloat16 on one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU with 500 power limit. We use tensor parallel size 1 and batch size 32. Sampling uses temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, at most 512 new tokens, and fixed seed (42). All methods use the same model, prompts, generation settings, and budget set = {1, 3, 4, 6, 8}. To test generalization (VII-G), we repeat the study on second GPU type, an NVIDIA L40S with 350 power limit, and with second model, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct [33], using the same precision (bfloat16), batch size, sampling settings, query sets, and load schedule. B. Datasets We use four datasets with different answer lengths: two math datasets with long answers, GSM8K [34] and MATH [35], and two multiple-choice datasets with short answers, ARCChallenge [36] and CommonsenseQA [37]. Each dataset has development set and test set of 500 queries each, which do not overlap; all reported results use the test sets. We report accuracy. All query sets and controller settings were frozen before we looked at the results, and we did no tuning afterwards. C. Compared Methods Fixed-4: standard self-consistency [2] with fixed budget: every answered query gets = 4 samples, and the plurality answer is returned. We use = 4 because it is the reference budget that defines Emax. Adaptive-Cal: adaptive budget allocation with offline calibration [8]. It chooses per query from offline accuracy and cost models, but does not use the live GPU state. ATEST-Calibrated (V-C): the offline mode of ATEST. ATEST-Online (V-B): the default mode of ATEST. Choice of baselines. Fixed-budget self-consistency is the base method that all self-consistency methods in Table build on, and Adaptive-Cal is the closest prior work, as the only one that models energy. The other adaptive methods stop sampling from reasoning signals alone, so their budget cannot react to GPU load; our ReasoningOnly-Strict ablation, which uses only such signal, keeps the same budget at every load level (VII-D). D. Controlled GPU Load To create shared-GPU setting, we run background load injector on the same GPU. It competes with the LLM for GPU resources, like other jobs on shared GPU. The injector is background thread that runs dense FP16 matrix multiplies on the same GPU for duty fraction of every 0.2 period and sleeps for the rest. We use four levels: idle (no injector), low, medium, and high, with injector duty settings of 0.25, 0.55, and 0.85. The duty setting controls how hard the injector works; it is not utilization target. We check the real effect with NVML [30]. For example, in the Fixed-4 runs the measured GPU utilization is about 0%, 24%, 54%, and 85%, and the average GPU power on GSM8K rises from 77 at idle to 431 at high load. The 500 queries of each run are split equally: 125 queries per load level, in the order idle, low, medium, high. The schedule is fixed by hash and is reused exactly for every method. So all methods see the same queries in the same order under the same injector settings. E. Energy Accounting and Budget We measure energy by GPU occupancy (Eocc). Each microbatch is charged for all the GPU energy used while it runs, computed from NVML power readings and its run time. When other jobs share the GPU, microbatch runs longer and the GPU draws more power, so its Eocc grows. We use this accounting because job on shared GPU holds the device for its whole run time, so this is the energy it is responsible for; the same accounting is used for all methods, so it does not favor any of them. Each run gets one shared energy budget Emax, set from the reference energy needed to run = 4 under the reference GPU condition. We set this budget separately for each GPU, model, and dataset, because the cost of sample depends on all three. All methods get the same budget. F. Metrics Quality and coverage. Accuracy is computed over all 500 queries; deferred query counts as wrong. Defer is the percentage of deferred queries. Sampling effort. Mean is the average budget. In overall results we count deferred query as = 0; in per-load results we average only over answered queries, so that the budget choice is visible. Energy. We report Eocc per query and joules per correct answer: J/correct = total Eocc number of correct answers . (12) This metric gets worse both when method spends energy on samples that do not help and when it gets fewer correct answers, for example by deferring queries. Budget safety. Budget used is total energy divided by Emax. value above 100% means the method overshot the budget. System performance. We report 95th-percentile (p95) latency per query, query throughput (queries per second, QPS), GPU utilization, and power. For ATEST-Online we also report the error of its online cost model as mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). G. Calibration Cost We measure the offline profiling of the calibrated methods separately, because it is paid before serving starts. Over four datasets, it uses 2,000 prompts, 80 settings, and 176,000 generated samples, for total of 5.73 GPU-hours and 7.16 MJ. ATEST-Online needs no dataset-specific profiling. H. Controlled Ablation In the main runs, the remaining budget shrinks over time, so change in could come from the budget and not from the load. To separate these effects, we run three versions of ATEST-Online: Full-HW (live GPU state and online cost learning), noHW-State (online cost learning, but the GPUstate input is hidden), and ReasoningOnly-Strict (no GPU state and online cost learning frozen). In this experiment we use large, non-binding energy budget and keep the remainingenergy value that the controller sees fixed. So the budget cannot drive the decision. VII. EVALUATION We organize the results around seven questions: Q1: Does ATEST-Online keep quality and serve every query under changing load? Q2: How does each controller react as load rises, and why does the offline mode defer? Q3: What does each mode cost in energy, including profiling? Q6: When is offline calibration the better choice? Q7: Does the behavior hold on another GPU and another model? A. Q1: Overall Results under Changing Load Table III gives the main results. Three points stand out. ATEST-Online serves every query. It has zero deferred queries on all four datasets and stays within the energy budget on all of them (budget used 92100%). Every other method defers queries on all four datasets, and Fixed-4 and AdaptiveCal also exceed the budget once each. ATEST-Online gives the best or tied-best accuracy. It has the highest accuracy on all four datasets: GSM8K (0.626), MATH (0.426), ARC-Challenge (0.794), and CommonsenseQA (0.716). Each result comes from one run of 500 queries, so the 95% confidence interval of one accuracy is about 4 points; gaps of up to about 3 points, as on GSM8K, MATH, and CommonsenseQA, are ties. The clear gains are on ARC-Challenge (+7.2 points over ATEST-Calibrated), where ATEST-Calibrated loses accuracy mainly because it defers 9.0% of the queries, and at high load (VII-B). ATEST-Online uses fewer samples. It has the lowest mean on three of four datasets, even though it answers more queries than any other method, because it stops as soon as the vote is stable. On MATH only Adaptive-Cal is lower, and only because it defers 55.2% of the queries. The two baselines do much worse on the long-answer datasets: Fixed-4 and Adaptive-Cal defer about half of the GSM8K and MATH queries, at every load level  (Fig. 4)  . Since each query may use only its share of the remaining budget, four samples often do not fit, so these baselines defer queries from the start. Answer to Q1: Yes. Under changing load, ATEST-Online answers every query, stays within budget, and gives the best or tied-best accuracy on all four datasets. B. Q2: Behavior as the Load Rises Fig. 4 shows each method at each load level. Both ATEST modes use fewer samples when the GPU is busy. ATEST-Online lowers its mean budget from idle to high load on all four datasets: from 2.09 to 1.00 on GSM8K, 2.10 to 1.00 on MATH, 2.14 to 1.51 on ARC-Challenge, and 3.37 to 2.54 on CommonsenseQA. ATEST-Calibrated also lowers its budget (for example, from 3.45 to 1.00 on GSM8K). Fixed-4 always uses = 4 for the queries it answers. ATEST-Online keeps serving at high load. On GSM8K at high load, both ATEST modes end up at = 1. But ATESTCalibrated defers 53 of the 125 queries (42.4%), so its accuracy for this phase falls to 44.0%. ATEST-Online answers all 125 queries with 60.0% accuracy and uses less energy per query (175.8 vs. 206.4 J). On MATH at high load the pattern is the same: ATEST-Calibrated defers 26.4% and reaches 39.2%, while ATEST-Online defers none and reaches 43.2%. Why does ATEST-Calibrated defer? We see two reasons in the measurements. First, it spends more early. At idle on GSM8K, ATEST-Calibrated uses = 3.45 and 124.4 per query, while ATEST-Online uses = 2.09 and 60.9 J. This buys higher idle accuracy (68.0% vs. 60.0%), but the budget is shared by the whole run, so less is left for the high-load phase, when each query is much more expensive. Second, its fixed cost model can be too pessimistic. ATEST-Calibrated admits query only if the predicted cost fits. On CommonsenseQA it deferred 23 queries although 21% of the energy budget was never used; on ARC-Challenge it deferred 45 queries with 15% unused. So the budget was not the limit here; the deferrals came from the controllers own cost predictions. Fig. 3(b) shows the root cause: the offline cost model is often far from the real cost under load. ATEST-Online avoids both problems because it measures every step and corrects its cost model as it goes. note on measured load. The injector settings are identical for all methods, but GPU utilization is sampled before each microbatch, so the reading depends on each methods execution pattern. On GSM8K and MATH, all methods see the same high-load utilization (about 85%); for ATEST-Online on ARCChallenge and CommonsenseQA the sampled reading at high load is lower (68% and 45%). We therefore base our main high-load comparison on GSM8K and MATH. Answer to Q2: As load rises, ATEST-Online lowers its budget and keeps serving every query. ATEST-Calibrated also lowers its budget, but its early spending and fixed cost model lead to deferrals at high load. C. Q3: Energy Cost, Including Profiling Serving energy. ATEST-Online has the lowest joules per correct answer on GSM8K (191.9 J) and MATH (371.2 J), Fig. 4. Behavior at each load level (125 queries per level). Top: accuracy over all queries (deferred = wrong). Middle: deferred queries (%). Bottom: mean over answered queries. ATEST-Online (blue, solid) never defers and lowers its budget as load rises. ATEST-Calibrated (orange, dashed) also lowers its budget, but it starts deferring at medium or high load on all four datasets, which pulls its accuracy down. TABLE IV END-TO-END COST OF THE TWO ATEST MODES ON FOUR DATASETS (2,000 QUERIES UNDER THE LOAD SCHEDULE). ATEST-CALIBRATED MUST PROFILE EVERY DATASET BEFORE SERVING. ATEST-ONLINE STARTS SERVING AT ONCE AND LEARNS ITS COST MODEL DURING SERVING, SO ITS LEARNING COST IS INCLUDED IN THE SERVING NUMBERS. On ARC-Challenge the two modes are almost equal (19.4 vs. 19.2 J). On CommonsenseQA, ATEST-Calibrated is more efficient (13.3 vs. 16.2 J, Table III), but it leaves 4.6% of the queries unanswered. So ATEST-Online is not always the cheapest per correct answer during serving, but it wins the overall trade-off: it gives higher accuracy, answers every query, and, once profiling is counted, uses far less total energy on every dataset. Setup cost versus serving cost. Table IV puts the full cost of both modes side by side. ATEST-Calibrated must profile every dataset before it can serve single query: 5.73 GPU-hours, 7.16 MJ, and 176,000 generated samples for our four datasets. Full-HW noHW-State ReasoningOnly-Strict Yes No No Yes Yes No Yes Yes No (B=3.12) ATEST-Online skips this stage completely and starts serving at once; its cost model learns during normal serving, so its learning cost is already inside the serving numbers. Serving itself costs almost the same for both modes (about 0.14 hours and 0.15 MJ for 2,000 queries), but ATEST-Online answers all 2,000 queries and gives 65 more correct answers. In total, ATEST-Calibrated uses about 42 more GPU time and 48 more energy than ATEST-Online in our study. Calibration is one-time cost per dataset, so long, stable deployment can spread it over many queries, but it must be repeated whenever the model, the GPU, the prompt format, or the workload changes. Answer to Q3: ATEST-Online is the most energy-efficient mode on the long-answer datasets. Including profiling, it uses 42 less GPU time and 48 less energy than ATESTCalibrated for the same 2,000 queries. D. Q4: Is the Adaptation Caused by Resource Signals? In the main runs, the energy budget shrinks over time. So the end-to-end results alone cannot tell us whether ATESTOnline lowers because of the load or because the budget is running out. The controlled ablation (VI-H) removes this TABLE VI RUNTIME BEHAVIOR OF THE TWO ATEST MODES UNDER THE LOAD SCHEDULE: P95 LATENCY PER QUERY (S), THROUGHPUT (QPS), AND THE ENERGY ERROR OF THE ONLINE COST MODEL OF ATEST-ONLINE (MAPE). ATEST-Calibrated ATEST-Online Dataset QPS p95 QPS MAPE GSM8K 0.509 MATH 1.019 ARC-C 0.130 0.086 CSQA 2.62 1.78 19.72 29.69 1.081 1.608 0.111 0.180 2.62 1.99 17.19 16. 23% 22% 134% 112% confound: the budget is large enough never to bind, and the remaining-energy value seen by the controller is fixed. Table shows the result. When both the GPU state and online cost learning are removed (ReasoningOnly-Strict), the controller uses the same mean budget, 3.12 samples per query at every load level on all four datasets. Its reasoning signal still changes from query to query, but without resource feedback its decisions do not react to the load at all. When online cost learning is on (noHW-State), the budget changes with the load even though the GPU-state input is hidden. This happens because the measured energy of each step already reflects the load. Adding the GPU state (Full-HW) changes the budgets again, most visibly on GSM8K and MATH. Resource awareness does not mean that must always go down when load goes up. The decision also depends on how stable the vote is. What the ablation shows is that removing the resource signals removes the controllers response to the load. Answer to Q4: Yes. With budget effects removed, online cost learning is necessary for the budget to follow the load, and the GPU state further changes the decisions. E. Q5: Runtime Overhead and Cost-Model Error Latency and throughput. Online control is not free (Table VI). ATEST-Online has higher p95 latency on three of four datasets, for example 1.08 vs. 0.51 on GSM8K and 0.18 vs. 0.09 on CommonsenseQA. Its throughput is about the same on GSM8K, higher on MATH, and lower on the two multiplechoice datasets, most clearly on CommonsenseQA (16.6 vs. 29.7 QPS). The reason is the step-by-step execution: ATESTOnline may run several small microbatches with decision between them, instead of one batch with all samples. For short answers, the fixed cost of each step is large compared with the generation time. Online cost-model error. The online cost model is updated after every step (671 to 993 updates per run). On the longanswer datasets its energy MAPE is moderate: 23% on GSM8K and 22% on MATH. On the short multiple-choice datasets it is much higher (134% on ARC-Challenge and 112% on CommonsenseQA). One likely reason is that step there uses only few joules, so small absolute errors become large relative errors. Even with this error, ATEST-Online never exceeded the energy budget. Two design choices help here: the safety margin βσE in Eq. (8), and the small step size, which limits the damage of one wrong prediction to one step. better cost model for very short steps is future work. Answer to Q5: The price of online control is higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks. The online cost model is accurate enough on long tasks and noisy on short ones, but the controller stays budget-safe. F. Q6: When Does Offline Calibration Win? Offline calibration is good choice when the GPU load is stable. In the idle phase of the load schedule, ATESTCalibrated matches or beats ATEST-Online in accuracy on all four datasets (for example, 68.0% vs. 60.0% on GSM8K and 42.4% vs. 39.2% on MATH). Table VIII shows separate run with no injected load at all. Here ATEST-Calibrated has higher accuracy than ATEST-Online on GSM8K (0.686 vs. 0.632), and they are close on the other datasets. Even Fixed-4 is strong in this setting: it has the lowest J/correct on three of four datasets. Answer to Q6: When the load is stable and the profile matches the runtime, offline calibration, or even well-chosen fixed budget, is hard to beat. The advantage of ATEST-Online appears when the load changes. G. Q7: Does the Behavior Hold on Another GPU and Another Model? We repeat the experiment on second GPU, an NVIDIA L40S, with Phi-3-mini and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on all four datasets. Everything else follows the A100 protocol; only Emax is re-measured, because the cost of sample depends on the GPU and the model. We compare Fixed-4 with ATEST-Online; ATEST-Calibrated and Adaptive-Cal would first need new offline profiling of every dataset on this GPU, which is exactly the cost that ATEST-Online avoids. Table VII shows the results. Zero deferrals. ATEST-Online answers every query in all eight new settings within the energy budget (9299.5% used), while Fixed-4 defers up to 48.8%. Accuracy. With Phi-3-mini, ATEST-Online reaches almost the same accuracy on the L40S as on the A100 (0.638 vs. 0.626 on GSM8K and 0.448 vs. 0.426 on MATH) and keeps its gains over Fixed-4: +13.2 points on GSM8K, +6.8 on MATH, and +12.0 on ARC-Challenge. With Qwen2.5-3B, it is more accurate than Fixed-4 on every dataset: it doubles GSM8K accuracy (0.138 to 0.280) and raises MATH from 0.242 to 0.348, ARCChallenge from 0.380 to 0.488, and CommonsenseQA from 0.414 to 0.564. Energy. ATEST-Online lowers joules per correct answer in seven of eight settings. With Phi-3-mini on the L40S, the drop is 22% on GSM8K (303.0 vs. 386.2 J), 16% on MATH, and 15% on ARC-Challenge; with Qwen2.5-3B it is larger, from 21% on ARC-Challenge to almost half on GSM8K (536 vs. 1019 J). When the budget is loose. The one exception is CommonsenseQA with Phi-3-mini on the L40S. Here the budget is loose enough for Fixed-4 to answer every query with = 4, and the two methods are almost equal (0.715 vs. 0.718 accuracy, 17.7 TABLE VII RESULTS ON SECOND GPU AND SECOND MODEL (500 QUERIES PER DATASET, SAME LOAD SCHEDULE, BUDGET RULE, AND FROZEN CONTROLLER SETTINGS). This agrees with Q6: online control helps most when the budget is tight. Answer to Q7: Yes. On second GPU and second model, ATEST-Online again answers every query within the budget, is at least as accurate as Fixed-4 in all eight settings, and uses less energy per correct answer in seven of them. VIII. DISCUSSION Which mode should be used? If the model, GPU, and workload stay the same and the load is stable, the profile of ATEST-Calibrated can be built once and reused, giving strong accuracy, low tail latency, and high throughput. If the GPU is shared, the load changes, or new datasets and models arrive often, ATEST-Online is the safer choice: it needs no profiling, follows the live cost, and serves every query. The two modes can also be combined by starting ATEST-Online from calibrated cost model. Service coverage is systems metric. controller can look good on the queries it answers while refusing many others, so we count deferred queries as wrong. On GSM8K at high load, this shows the real difference: 44.0% accuracy with 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated, against 60.0% with none for ATEST-Online. Resource awareness is more than use fewer samples when busy. ATEST-Online compares the value of the next step with its current cost: it stops on stable vote even on an idle GPU, and continues on split vote even under load if the cost is acceptable. Why not let an LLM decide? variant in which an LLM makes the continue-or-stop decision reached similar accuracy, but exceeded the energy budget on three of four datasets (by up to 6.2% on GSM8K) and spent extra GPU energy on its decisions. small numerical controller is cheaper and easier to keep within hard budget. IX. LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK Evaluation scope. Our evaluation is bounded by the available compute. Every setting must be run for every method and load level, together with the stable-load runs, the ablations, and the offline calibration, so the total GPU time grows quickly. We therefore use 500 queries per dataset, four datasets, two open models, and two GPU types, which is enough to compare all methods under the same conditions. Runtime overhead. Step-by-step control adds some overhead on short tasks (VII-E). Batching the steps of several queries and overlapping decisions with generation could reduce it. Online cost model. The online cost model of ATEST-Online is simple by design. Richer online models could make cost predictions more precise. Integration with inference systems. ATEST decides how much reasoning each query gets, while inference engines and power managers decide how that work runs. Running ATEST inside engines such as vLLM [10] or with GPU frequency control [28] could manage both together. X. CONCLUSION The cost of test-time scaling sample is not fixed on shared GPU; in our measurements it changes by up to 4.1 with load. We presented ATEST, which makes the sampling decision depend on both the value of more reasoning and its current cost. Its default mode, ATEST-Online, learns the cost online, decides step by step, and needs no profiling; its offline mode, ATEST-Calibrated, works well when the load is stable and one profile can be reused. Under changing load on four datasets, ATEST-Online answered every query, stayed within the energy budget, and gave the highest or tied-best accuracy, while the offline mode deferred up to 42.4% of queries at high load. The same behavior held on an L40S GPU and with second model, Qwen2.5-3B. It also avoided 5.73 GPU-hours of offline calibration. controlled ablation showed that online cost learning is what makes the budget follow the load. The price is higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks. Our results suggest that test-time scaling on shared accelerators should be treated as runtime resource-management problem, not only as reasoning problem.
